subject: Meteorology
description: SACAA PPL Meteorology question bank covering atmosphere, temperature, pressure, humidity, clouds, visibility, fronts, weather systems, South African weather, and aviation weather reports.

questions.question: The volume of oxygen in the atmosphere is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The atmosphere is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases (argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour, etc.). The oxygen percentage remains constant up to about 70,000 ft, though the partial pressure of oxygen decreases with altitude.

questions.question: An aircraft is flying at FL095, OAT +5°C. The temperature deviation from ISA is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at FL095 (9,500 ft): 15°C - (9.5 × 2°C) = 15 - 19 = -4°C. Actual OAT is +5°C. Deviation = actual - ISA = +5 - (-4) = +9°C. The air is 9°C warmer than standard.

questions.question: The layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere is called:-
questions.explanation: The tropopause is the boundary between the troposphere (where most weather occurs) and the stratosphere above. Its height varies from about 28,000 ft at the poles to 56,000 ft at the equator. Temperature stops decreasing at the tropopause and remains constant or increases in the stratosphere.

questions.question: Air has a tendency to flow from:-

options.text: an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure
an area of low pressure to an area of high pressure
warm areas to cold areas only
the equator to the poles only

questions.explanation: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure due to the pressure gradient force. This is the primary force that causes wind. The greater the pressure difference (steeper the gradient), the stronger the wind. Other forces (Coriolis, friction) modify the direction of this flow.

questions.question: The average height of the troposphere:-

options.text: is the same at all latitudes

questions.explanation: The troposphere extends to about 56,000 ft (16 km) at the equator but only about 28,000 ft (8 km) at the poles. This is because the strong solar heating at the equator causes vigorous convection that pushes the tropopause higher. The average height at mid-latitudes is about 36,000 ft (11 km).

questions.question: In a temperature inversion:-

options.text: the temperature increases with an increase in height
the temperature decreases rapidly with height
the lapse rate is steeper than normal

questions.explanation: A temperature inversion is a reversal of the normal lapse rate — temperature increases with altitude instead of decreasing. Inversions are very stable layers that suppress convection, trap pollutants and moisture below them, and can cause poor visibility, fog, and smooth flying conditions.

questions.question: Dewpoint temperature is the temperature at which:-

options.text: air will become saturated at a constant pressure

questions.explanation: The dewpoint is the temperature to which air must be cooled (at constant pressure) for it to become saturated (100% relative humidity). When air temperature equals dewpoint, condensation occurs — forming cloud, fog, or dew. A small temperature-dewpoint spread indicates high humidity and a risk of fog or low cloud.

questions.question: Instability in the atmosphere is associated with:-

options.text: a steep positive environmental lapse rate

questions.explanation: A steep environmental lapse rate (temperature decreasing rapidly with height) means a rising parcel of air remains warmer than its surroundings and continues to rise — this is instability. It leads to convective activity, cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and showery precipitation. The steeper the lapse rate, the greater the instability.

questions.question: The term 'insolation' or 'solar radiation' is used to define the:-

options.text: heating of the earth's surface by the sun
re-radiation of heat from the earth's surface
heating of the atmosphere directly by the sun

questions.explanation: Insolation (incoming solar radiation) refers to the sun's energy reaching and heating the earth's surface. The atmosphere is largely transparent to short-wave solar radiation, so the sun heats the ground first. The ground then re-radiates this energy as long-wave (terrestrial) radiation, which heats the atmosphere from below.

questions.question: In terms of visibility, the difference between fog and mist is that:-

options.text: fog has a visibility of less than 1000 metres
mist has a visibility of less than 1000 metres

questions.explanation: Fog is defined as visibility less than 1000 metres due to suspended water droplets. Mist is visibility between 1000 and 5000 metres. Both are caused by the same process (condensation near the surface), but fog is denser. Haze is reduced visibility due to dry particles (dust, smoke).

questions.question: Adiabatic process is the term used to describe:-

options.text: the cooling of air as it rises and expands without exchanging heat with its surroundings
the heating of air by the sun
the transfer of heat by conduction

questions.explanation: An adiabatic process occurs without heat exchange with the environment. Rising air expands (lower pressure at altitude) and cools adiabatically. Unsaturated air cools at the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) of 3°C/1000 ft. Saturated air cools at the Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR) of approximately 1.5°C/1000 ft.

questions.question: Relative humidity:-

options.text: decreases with an increase in temperature
increases with an increase in temperature

questions.explanation: Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour content to the maximum the air can hold at that temperature. Warmer air can hold more moisture, so if temperature increases (with the same moisture content), relative humidity decreases. Conversely, cooling the air increases relative humidity until saturation (100%) is reached.

questions.question: According to Buys Ballot's Law, an observer standing with their back to the wind in the Southern Hemisphere will have:-
questions.explanation: Buys Ballot's Law: In the Southern Hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind — low pressure is on your right. This is because the Coriolis force deflects wind to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, so wind flows clockwise around a low. In the Northern Hemisphere, low pressure is on the left.

questions.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, the wind around a low pressure system blows:-

options.text: clockwise with the area of lowest pressure in the centre
anticlockwise with the area of lowest pressure in the centre
clockwise with the highest pressure in the centre

questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind flows clockwise around a low pressure system (cyclone) and spirals inward. This is due to the Coriolis force deflecting the wind to the left. In the Northern Hemisphere, the circulation is anticlockwise around a low. The pressure is lowest at the centre of the system.

questions.question: The Coriolis Force is created by:-

options.text: the gravitational pull of the moon

questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is an apparent force caused by the earth's rotation. It deflects moving air to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. It is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles. It affects wind direction but not wind speed.

questions.question: A land breeze will be found at coastal areas:-
questions.explanation: At night, the land cools faster than the sea. The air over the warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land flows out to sea to replace it — this is a land breeze. It is the reverse of the sea breeze (which occurs during the day when the land is warmer than the sea).

questions.question: During summer in Southern Africa, the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is generally located:-
questions.explanation: The ITCZ follows the sun's zenith position with a lag. During the Southern Hemisphere summer (December-February), the ITCZ moves south of the equator, bringing moist, unstable conditions, thunderstorms, and heavy rainfall to southern Africa. In winter, it moves north of the equator.

questions.question: The type of wind which flows upslope during the day is called:-
questions.explanation: An anabatic wind flows upslope during the day. The sun heats the mountain slope, which heats the air in contact with it. This warm air rises up the slope, creating an upslope (anabatic) wind. At night, the reverse occurs — cooled air flows downslope as a katabatic wind.

questions.question: A 'trough' is:-

options.text: a wedge or elongation of low pressure

questions.explanation: A trough is an elongated area of low pressure extending from a low pressure centre. It is the opposite of a ridge (elongated high pressure). Troughs are associated with convergence, rising air, cloud development, and often precipitation. Wind shifts occur as a trough passes.

questions.question: A sea breeze will be found at coastal areas:-
questions.explanation: During the day, the land heats faster than the sea. Air over the warm land rises, and cooler air from the sea flows inland to replace it — this is a sea breeze. Sea breezes typically develop mid-morning and are strongest in the afternoon. They can extend 15-30 km inland.

questions.question: In a high pressure system in the Southern Hemisphere:-

options.text: the wind rotates anticlockwise with an outward and downward flow
the wind rotates clockwise with an inward and upward flow
the wind rotates anticlockwise with an inward flow

questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind flows anticlockwise around a high pressure system (anticyclone) and spirals outward. Air subsides (descends) in the centre, warming adiabatically, which suppresses cloud formation and generally produces fine, stable weather. This is the opposite of low pressure circulation.

questions.question: Cirrus type cloud refers to:-

options.text: high thin cloud composed of ice crystals

questions.explanation: Cirrus clouds are high-level clouds (above 20,000 ft) composed entirely of ice crystals. They appear as thin, wispy, white streaks or filaments. Cirrus can indicate the approach of a warm front (when thickening progressively). Other high clouds include cirrostratus (thin sheet) and cirrocumulus (small white patches).

questions.question: The type of cloud which is formed by convection is called:-
questions.explanation: Cumulus clouds form through convection — warm air rising from the heated surface. They have a flat base (at the condensation level) and a cauliflower-like top. Fair weather cumulus indicates instability. If convection is strong enough, cumulus can develop into towering cumulus and eventually cumulonimbus (thunderstorm clouds).

questions.question: Nimbostratus cloud is:-

options.text: commonly associated with a warm front

questions.explanation: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark grey, layered cloud that produces continuous moderate to heavy precipitation. It is most commonly associated with warm fronts, where warm air rises slowly over a wedge of cold air, producing widespread stratiform cloud and steady rain over a large area.

questions.question: Cumulonimbus cloud is characterised by:-
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus (Cb) is the thunderstorm cloud. It is characterised by severe turbulence, heavy precipitation (rain, hail), lightning, strong up- and downdrafts, wind shear, microbursts, and icing. Cb clouds can extend from near the surface to the tropopause. They should be avoided by at least 10 NM.

questions.question: On a clear night, light winds and moist air blowing over the land will most probably create:-
questions.explanation: Radiation fog forms on clear nights when the ground loses heat by radiation, cooling the air in contact with it to its dewpoint. Light winds (2-8 kt) provide gentle mixing to deepen the fog layer. Clear skies allow maximum radiative cooling. Moist air (small temperature-dewpoint spread) reaches saturation quickly.

questions.question: The ideal conditions for the formation of advection fog are:-

options.text: warm moist air blowing over a cold surface
cold air blowing over a warm surface

questions.explanation: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves horizontally over a colder surface. The cold surface cools the air to its dewpoint, causing condensation. Unlike radiation fog, advection fog can form in moderate winds and overcast conditions. It is common along coastlines where warm air flows over cold ocean currents.

questions.question: The factor most likely to cause a decrease in the stability of an air mass is:-

options.text: warming of the air mass from below
cooling of the air mass from below

questions.explanation: Warming from below steepens the environmental lapse rate, making the air mass less stable (more unstable). The heated surface air becomes buoyant and wants to rise. This is why convective activity and thunderstorms are most common in the afternoon when surface heating is greatest.

questions.question: A cold front approaching South Africa will be characterised by:-
questions.explanation: Ahead of a cold front in South Africa, the warm sector air flows from the north-west (pre-frontal winds). As the cold front passes, the wind veers to the south-west or south. The north-westerly pre-frontal wind is often warm and may bring cloud and rain before the front arrives.

questions.question: The type of clouds which typically characterise a cold front are:-
questions.explanation: Cold fronts are characterised by cumuliform clouds (cumulus and cumulonimbus) because the cold air undercuts the warm air rapidly, forcing it to rise steeply. This produces convective clouds, heavy showers, thunderstorms, turbulence, and gusty winds. The weather band is narrow but intense.

questions.question: A front caused by cold air cutting under warm air is referred to as:-
questions.explanation: A cold front occurs when a mass of cold air advances and undercuts warmer air, forcing it to rise. The cold air is denser and pushes under the warm air like a wedge. Cold fronts typically move faster than warm fronts and produce more intense but shorter-duration weather.

questions.question: The indications of the approach of a warm front are:-

options.text: cirrus followed by cirrostratus or altostratus type clouds

questions.explanation: A warm front approaches gradually. The first sign is high cirrus cloud, followed by cirrostratus (halo around sun/moon), then altostratus (sun becomes dim), then nimbostratus with continuous rain. The cloud base lowers progressively as the front approaches. This sequence can take 12-24 hours.

questions.question: The symbol SCT is used to indicate:-
questions.explanation: Cloud cover abbreviations: FEW = 1-2 oktas, SCT (scattered) = 3-4 oktas, BKN (broken) = 5-7 oktas, OVC (overcast) = 8 oktas. One okta = one-eighth of the sky covered. These abbreviations are used in METARs and TAFs to describe cloud amount.

questions.question: The symbol FEW is used to indicate:-
questions.explanation: FEW indicates 1-2 oktas (eighths) of sky covered by cloud. This means the sky is mostly clear with only a small amount of cloud. The cloud amount hierarchy is: FEW (1-2), SCT (3-4), BKN (5-7), OVC (8 oktas).

questions.question: The term CAVOK is used in weather forecasts to indicate:-

options.text: visibility 10 km or more and no cloud below 5000 ft

questions.explanation: CAVOK (Ceiling And Visibility OK) is used when: visibility is 10 km or more, no cloud below 5000 ft or below the highest minimum sector altitude (whichever is greater), no cumulonimbus at any level, and no significant weather. It replaces the visibility, cloud, and weather groups in a METAR/TAF.

questions.question: The information provided by the ATIS includes:-

options.text: the airfield's surface wind, QNH, visibility, and runway in use

questions.explanation: ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) is a continuous broadcast providing: aerodrome identification, time, runway in use, surface wind, visibility, cloud, temperature, dewpoint, QNH, and any significant information (e.g., runway works, NOTAMs). Each update is identified by a phonetic letter (Alpha, Bravo, etc.).

questions.question: In winter, an aeroplane which has been parked outside during a night with clear skies may expect to be covered with:-
questions.explanation: Hoar frost (ground frost) forms on cold, clear nights when the aircraft skin cools by radiation to below the dewpoint and below 0°C. Water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals on the surface (sublimation). Hoar frost must be completely removed before flight as it disrupts airflow and reduces lift.

questions.question: The characteristics of a moist, unstable air mass include:-
questions.explanation: A moist unstable air mass produces: cumuliform clouds (cumulus, cumulonimbus), showery precipitation (heavy but intermittent), good visibility between showers, turbulence, and gusty surface winds. This contrasts with a stable air mass which produces stratiform clouds, continuous light precipitation, and poor visibility.

questions.question: The characteristics of a stable air mass include:-

options.text: poor surface visibility and stratiform clouds

questions.explanation: A stable air mass suppresses vertical motion, producing: stratiform clouds (stratus, stratocumulus), continuous light precipitation (drizzle), poor surface visibility (haze, mist, fog trapped below inversions), smooth flying conditions, and little turbulence. Pollutants and moisture are trapped near the surface.

questions.question: A concave or almond-shaped cloud which appears to be stationary in the vicinity of mountains is called:-
questions.explanation: Lenticular (lens-shaped) clouds form in the crests of standing waves (mountain waves) downwind of mountain ranges. They appear stationary because they form continuously on the upwind side and dissipate on the downwind side. They indicate strong mountain wave activity and severe turbulence.

questions.question: Whilst flying in the vicinity of a mountain range a pilot observes formations of static lenticular cloud. The pilot should expect:-
questions.explanation: Lenticular clouds indicate mountain wave activity with potentially severe turbulence. Mountain waves can produce updrafts and downdrafts exceeding 2000 ft/min, severe to extreme turbulence (especially in the rotor zone below the wave crests), and can extend well above the mountain tops. Avoid flying near lenticular clouds.

questions.question: In stable conditions, with a strong wind blowing over a mountain range or high ridge of hills:-

options.text: mountain wave turbulence is to be expected
only light turbulence near the surface

questions.explanation: Mountain waves form when stable air is forced over a mountain barrier by strong winds (typically >25 kt) blowing roughly perpendicular to the ridge. The air oscillates in a wave pattern downwind, producing severe turbulence, particularly in the rotor zone. Waves can extend to the stratosphere.

questions.question: The most hazardous type of thunderstorms to aircraft are:-
questions.explanation: Embedded thunderstorms (Cb hidden within layers of stratiform cloud) are the most hazardous because they cannot be seen visually and may not be detected until the aircraft is already in them. The pilot has no visual warning to avoid them. Frontal Cb embedded in nimbostratus or altostratus is particularly dangerous.

questions.question: The greatest intensity of a thunderstorm occurs during:-
questions.explanation: A thunderstorm has three stages: (1) Cumulus/developing — mainly updrafts, (2) Mature — both updrafts and downdrafts coexist, producing the most severe weather (heaviest rain, hail, lightning, strongest turbulence, microbursts), (3) Dissipating — mainly downdrafts, storm weakens. The mature stage is the most dangerous.

questions.question: When flying from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure:-

options.text: the altimeter will tend to over-read
the altimeter will tend to under-read

questions.explanation: Flying from high to low pressure without updating the QNH causes the altimeter to over-read (show higher than actual altitude). The aircraft is actually lower than indicated — 'High to Low, look out below.' This is dangerous for terrain clearance. Always obtain and set the current QNH.

questions.question: A METAR is:-

options.text: a report of actual weather at an aerodrome
a weather forecast for an aerodrome

questions.explanation: A METAR (Meteorological Aerodrome Report) is an observation of actual weather conditions at an aerodrome at a specific time. It includes: wind, visibility, weather phenomena, cloud, temperature, dewpoint, and QNH. METARs are issued every 30 minutes or hourly. A SPECI is a special METAR issued when conditions change significantly.

questions.question: A TAF is:-

options.text: a weather forecast for an aerodrome

questions.explanation: A TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) is a forecast of expected weather conditions at an aerodrome. It covers a period of 9, 24, or 30 hours and includes: wind, visibility, weather, and cloud. Changes are indicated by BECMG (becoming), TEMPO (temporary), or PROB (probability) groups.

questions.question: Air density will:-

options.text: decrease with an increase in humidity
increase with an increase in humidity

questions.explanation: Water vapour is lighter than dry air (molecular weight of water = 18, dry air ≈ 29). When water vapour replaces dry air molecules, the air becomes less dense. Therefore, humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure. This reduces aircraft performance (less lift, less engine power).

questions.question: The term veering refers to:-

options.text: a wind that is changing in a clockwise direction
a wind that is changing in an anticlockwise direction
a wind that is increasing in speed
a wind that is decreasing in speed

questions.explanation: Veering means the wind direction is changing clockwise (e.g., from north to east to south). Backing means the wind is changing anticlockwise (e.g., from north to west to south). In the Southern Hemisphere, wind backs with the passage of a cold front (e.g., NW to SW).

questions.question: The term backing refers to:-

options.text: a wind that is changing in an anticlockwise direction
a wind that is changing in a clockwise direction
a wind that is decreasing in speed

questions.explanation: Backing means the wind direction is changing anticlockwise (e.g., from west to south to east). This is the opposite of veering (clockwise change). Wind direction changes are important indicators of frontal passage and pressure system movement.

questions.question: The flow of air from a high to a low in the Southern Hemisphere is deflected by the Coriolis force:-
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects moving air to the left of its direction of travel. This is why wind flows clockwise around a low pressure system and anticlockwise around a high pressure system in the Southern Hemisphere. In the Northern Hemisphere, deflection is to the right.

questions.question: Following the passage of a cold front:-

options.text: the pressure will begin to rise
the pressure will continue to fall

questions.explanation: After a cold front passes, the cold air behind the front is denser and the pressure rises. Other post-frontal changes include: temperature drops, wind backs (in the Southern Hemisphere, e.g., NW to SW), visibility improves, cloud clears, and showers diminish. The rising pressure is a key indicator of frontal passage.

questions.question: The presence of a coastal low on the east coast of South Africa may be characterised by:-

options.text: overcast conditions with light rain or drizzle

questions.explanation: Coastal lows along the South African east coast bring overcast conditions with low stratus or stratocumulus cloud, light rain or drizzle, poor visibility, and moderate to strong onshore winds. They form when air flows off the interior plateau and is replaced by moist maritime air along the coast.

questions.question: The characteristics of the South African summer include:-

options.text: the presence of moist south-easterly trade winds
cold fronts affecting the entire country

questions.explanation: During the South African summer (October-March), moist south-easterly trade winds bring moisture from the Indian Ocean over the eastern parts of the country. This, combined with surface heating, produces afternoon thunderstorms over the interior (highveld). The ITCZ moves south, enhancing moisture convergence.

questions.question: According to ISA, the sea level density of the air is:-

options.text: 1225 grams per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
1225 grams per cubic metre and increases with altitude

questions.explanation: ISA sea level density is 1.225 kg/m³ (1225 g/m³). Density decreases with altitude because pressure decreases (fewer air molecules per unit volume). Density also decreases with increasing temperature and increasing humidity. Density altitude is the key performance parameter for aircraft operations.

questions.question: The term 'lapse rate' is used to describe:-

options.text: the decrease in temperature with altitude
the increase in pressure with altitude
the change in wind speed with altitude
the decrease in humidity with altitude

questions.explanation: Lapse rate is the rate at which temperature decreases with increasing altitude. The ISA lapse rate is approximately 2°C per 1000 ft. The environmental (actual) lapse rate varies and determines atmospheric stability. If the actual lapse rate is steeper than the DALR (3°C/1000 ft), the atmosphere is absolutely unstable.

questions.question: In the Southern Hemisphere, an aircraft which is being subjected to left drift is:-

options.text: flying towards an area of low pressure
flying towards an area of high pressure

questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind flows clockwise around a low. If an aircraft experiences left drift, the wind is coming from the right. Using Buys Ballot's Law (back to wind, low on right in SH), the low pressure is to the left — meaning the aircraft is flying towards the low pressure area.

questions.question: The type of cloud which can be expected to form as a result of a moist unstable air mass being forced upwards is:-
questions.explanation: When moist unstable air is forced to rise (by orographic lift, fronts, or convergence), it continues to rise vigorously once triggered. This produces clouds with great vertical development — towering cumulus and cumulonimbus. These bring heavy showers, thunderstorms, turbulence, and potentially hail.

questions.question: The weather conditions associated with a ridge of high pressure include:-
questions.explanation: A ridge of high pressure is an elongated area of high pressure. Air subsides (descends) within it, warming adiabatically and suppressing cloud formation. This generally produces fine weather, light winds, good visibility (unless trapped pollution), and stable conditions. Ridges often bring temporary fine spells between frontal systems.

questions.question: Virga is:-

options.text: rain which evaporates before it reaches the surface

questions.explanation: Virga is precipitation that falls from a cloud but evaporates before reaching the ground. It appears as streaks or wisps hanging below the cloud base. Virga can indicate dry air below the cloud and may be associated with microbursts (the evaporation cools the air, creating strong downdrafts).

questions.question: Rime ice may be expected to form on an aircraft:-

options.text: when supercooled drops of water freeze on impact
in clear air above the freezing level

questions.explanation: Rime ice forms when small supercooled water droplets freeze instantly on contact with the aircraft. It has a rough, white, opaque appearance (trapped air). It forms in stratiform clouds with small droplets at temperatures between 0°C and -20°C. Clear ice forms from larger droplets that spread before freezing, and is more dangerous.

questions.question: Coastal lows along the South African coast are generally created by:-

options.text: a strong flow of air from the interior

questions.explanation: Coastal lows form when strong offshore (berg) winds flow from the interior plateau to the coast. As the air descends the escarpment, it warms adiabatically and creates a low pressure area along the coast. Moist maritime air is then drawn in from the sea, producing low cloud, drizzle, and poor visibility.

questions.question: Cooling of the earth's surface during the night:-

options.text: is greatest during clear skies over rocky or desert areas
is the same regardless of cloud cover

questions.explanation: Radiative cooling is greatest under clear skies (no cloud to re-radiate heat back to the surface) over rocky or desert surfaces (low specific heat capacity — they lose heat quickly). Cloud acts as a blanket, trapping heat. Water surfaces cool slowly due to high specific heat capacity.

questions.question: A warm, dry wind blowing down a mountain during the day is a typical characteristic of:-
questions.explanation: The föhn (foehn) wind occurs when moist air is forced over a mountain. It rises on the windward side, cooling at the SALR (slow rate due to condensation releasing latent heat), loses moisture as precipitation, then descends on the leeward side warming at the DALR (faster rate). The result is a warm, dry wind on the lee side.

questions.question: An air mass which is approaching South Africa from the Antarctic is classified as:-
questions.explanation: Air masses approaching South Africa from the south (Antarctic region) travel over the ocean and are classified as polar maritime (mP). They are cold and moist. As they move northward over warmer waters, they become unstable in the lower layers, producing cumulus clouds and showers.

questions.question: As a polar maritime air mass passes over South Africa during summer it will:-

options.text: absorb heat in the lower layers and become unstable

questions.explanation: During summer, the South African land surface is warm. A cold polar maritime air mass passing over this warm surface is heated from below, steepening the lapse rate and becoming unstable. This produces convective clouds (cumulus), showers, good visibility between showers, and turbulence.

questions.question: Convergence is associated with:-

options.text: rising air and a low pressure system with instability

questions.explanation: Convergence occurs when air flows together from different directions. Since air cannot accumulate at the surface, it is forced to rise. This rising air cools, may reach saturation, and forms clouds. Convergence is associated with low pressure systems, fronts, troughs, and the ITCZ. It promotes instability and precipitation.

questions.question: An occluded front occurs when:-

options.text: a cold front overtakes a warm front

questions.explanation: An occlusion forms when a faster-moving cold front catches up with and overtakes a slower warm front. The warm air is lifted off the surface entirely. Occluded fronts can produce a combination of warm and cold front weather — widespread cloud, precipitation, and sometimes embedded thunderstorms.

questions.question: The south-westerly buster which affects the coast of KwaZulu-Natal is caused by:-

options.text: the anticyclonic flow of air from a high pressure system ridging in behind a coastal low

questions.explanation: The south-westerly buster (or southwesterly buster) occurs along the KZN coast when a high pressure system ridges around behind a coastal low. The strong pressure gradient between the high and the coastal low produces sudden strong south-westerly winds, rough seas, and a rapid drop in temperature.

questions.question: The Black South Easter is a wind which occurs in South Africa when:-

options.text: there is a well-developed high pressure system to the west of Cape Town with strong pressure gradients and a long sea track
a cold front passes over Cape Town

questions.explanation: The Black South Easter occurs in the Cape when a strong high pressure system lies south or west of Cape Town. The strong pressure gradient drives a powerful south-easterly wind. The long sea track allows the air to pick up moisture, which condenses as orographic cloud over Table Mountain (the 'tablecloth'). It can reach gale force.

questions.question: The South African Berg Wind is generally caused by:-

options.text: a strong high pressure system over southern Africa

questions.explanation: Berg winds occur when a strong high pressure system over the interior of South Africa drives air from the high plateau down the escarpment to the coast. As the air descends, it warms adiabatically (DALR), arriving at the coast as a hot, dry wind. Berg winds often precede cold fronts and can cause extreme fire danger.

questions.question: When the standard pressure setting, 1013 hPa, is set on the altimeter subscale, the altimeter will indicate:-
questions.explanation: Setting 1013.25 hPa (standard pressure) on the altimeter gives pressure altitude — the altitude in the ISA corresponding to the measured pressure. This is used for flight level assignments above the transition altitude. All aircraft use the same reference, ensuring consistent vertical separation.

questions.question: Density altitude is:-

options.text: derived by correcting the pressure altitude for temperature
the altitude above mean sea level

questions.explanation: Density altitude = pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. It represents the altitude in the ISA at which the current air density would be found. High density altitude (hot, high, humid) means reduced aircraft performance — longer take-off runs, reduced climb rates, and reduced engine power.

questions.question: When QFE is set on the altimeter subscale, the instrument will read:-

options.text: zero on the ground at the aerodrome
the altitude above mean sea level

questions.explanation: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the aerodrome elevation. When set on the altimeter, it reads zero on the ground at that aerodrome and indicates height above the aerodrome during flight. QFE is useful for circuit operations where height above the field is the primary reference.

questions.question: When QNH has been set on the altimeter subscale, the instrument will indicate:-

options.text: the aircraft's altitude above mean sea level
the aircraft's height above the aerodrome

questions.explanation: QNH is the atmospheric pressure at mean sea level for a given location. When set on the altimeter, it indicates altitude above mean sea level (AMSL). On the ground at the aerodrome, the altimeter should read the aerodrome elevation. QNH is the standard setting for flight below the transition altitude.

questions.question: The Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The DALR is the rate at which unsaturated (dry) air cools as it rises — approximately 3°C per 1000 ft (or 9.8°C per 1000 m). This rate is constant regardless of the actual temperature. It applies until the air reaches its dewpoint and condensation begins, after which the SALR applies.

questions.question: The Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR) is approximately:-
questions.explanation: The SALR is the rate at which saturated air cools as it rises — approximately 1.5°C per 1000 ft (varies between 1.1°C and 2.8°C depending on temperature and moisture content). It is less than the DALR because condensation releases latent heat, partially offsetting the cooling due to expansion.

questions.question: If the Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR) is greater than the DALR, the atmosphere is:-
questions.explanation: If the ELR exceeds the DALR (>3°C/1000 ft), any rising parcel of air — whether saturated or unsaturated — will always be warmer than its surroundings and will continue to rise. This is absolute instability, leading to vigorous convection, cumulonimbus development, and severe weather.

questions.question: If the Environmental Lapse Rate is less than the SALR, the atmosphere is:-
questions.explanation: If the ELR is less than the SALR (<1.5°C/1000 ft), any rising parcel of air — whether saturated or unsaturated — will always be cooler than its surroundings and will sink back. This is absolute stability. Inversions (negative lapse rate) are the most extreme form of stability.

questions.question: Conditional instability exists when the ELR is:-

options.text: between the SALR and the DALR

questions.explanation: When the ELR is between the SALR (~1.5°C/1000 ft) and the DALR (~3°C/1000 ft), the atmosphere is conditionally unstable. Unsaturated air is stable (cools faster than the environment), but if forced to rise to its condensation level and become saturated, it becomes unstable (cools slower than the environment). This is the most common state.

questions.question: The height of the cloud base can be estimated using the formula:-
questions.explanation: The cloud base height can be estimated by multiplying the temperature-dewpoint spread (in °C) by 400. For example, if temperature is 20°C and dewpoint is 12°C, the spread is 8°C, and the estimated cloud base is 8 × 400 = 3200 ft AGL. This works because temperature decreases at 3°C/1000 ft and dewpoint at about 0.5°C/1000 ft.

questions.question: Stratus cloud is characterised by:-

options.text: a uniform grey layer with a relatively flat base

questions.explanation: Stratus is a low-level, uniform, grey, sheet-like cloud with a flat base. It forms in stable conditions, often by the lifting of fog or cooling of air below an inversion. It may produce drizzle or light rain but not heavy precipitation. Stratus can reduce visibility and create low ceilings, making VFR flight difficult.

questions.question: Altocumulus and altostratus clouds are classified as:-
questions.explanation: Cloud classification by height: Low (surface to 6500 ft) — stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus. Medium (6500-20000 ft) — altostratus, altocumulus. High (above 20000 ft) — cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus. Clouds of vertical development (cumulus, cumulonimbus) span multiple levels.

questions.question: Wind shear is defined as:-

options.text: a sudden change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance
a steady increase in wind speed with altitude
the difference between surface wind and gradient wind

questions.explanation: Wind shear is a sudden change in wind velocity (speed and/or direction) over a short distance, either horizontally or vertically. It is hazardous to aircraft, particularly during take-off and landing. Sources include thunderstorms (microbursts), fronts, temperature inversions, and low-level jets.

questions.question: A microburst is:-

options.text: a localised, intense downdraft from a thunderstorm that spreads outward on contact with the ground
a small area of high pressure
a sudden increase in wind speed at altitude

questions.explanation: A microburst is a small-scale, intense downdraft that, on reaching the surface, produces damaging divergent winds. It can cause a sudden loss of airspeed and altitude — extremely dangerous during take-off and landing. Microbursts last 5-15 minutes and can produce wind speed changes of 45 kt or more across a short distance.

questions.question: The geostrophic wind blows:-

options.text: from high to low pressure directly

questions.explanation: The geostrophic wind is the theoretical wind that results from a balance between the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force. It blows parallel to straight isobars. In reality, surface friction causes the actual wind to cross the isobars at an angle (about 30° over land, 10° over sea) toward low pressure.

questions.question: Surface friction causes the wind to:-

options.text: blow across the isobars at an angle toward low pressure
blow exactly parallel to the isobars

questions.explanation: Surface friction slows the wind, reducing the Coriolis force (which depends on wind speed). The pressure gradient force then dominates, causing the wind to cross the isobars at an angle toward low pressure. Over land (more friction), the angle is about 30°. Over sea (less friction), it is about 10°.

questions.question: The wind at 2000 ft above the surface compared to the surface wind will generally be:-

options.text: stronger and backed (in the Southern Hemisphere)

questions.explanation: Above the friction layer (approximately 2000 ft AGL), friction effects diminish. The wind speed increases (less friction to slow it) and the direction backs in the Southern Hemisphere (becomes more parallel to the isobars). In the Northern Hemisphere, the wind veers with altitude above the friction layer.

questions.question: Haze is caused by:-

options.text: dry particles such as dust, smoke, or sand suspended in the air

questions.explanation: Haze is reduced visibility caused by dry particles (dust, smoke, sand, pollution) suspended in the air. It gives a bluish or yellowish tinge. Haze is common in stable conditions where particles are trapped below an inversion. It differs from mist and fog, which are caused by water droplets.

questions.question: The BKN cloud cover abbreviation indicates:-
questions.explanation: BKN (broken) indicates 5-7 oktas of cloud cover. This means more than half the sky is covered but some blue sky is visible. BKN is the minimum cloud amount that constitutes a 'ceiling' for aviation purposes. The hierarchy is: FEW (1-2), SCT (3-4), BKN (5-7), OVC (8).

questions.question: The OVC cloud cover abbreviation indicates:-
questions.explanation: OVC (overcast) indicates 8 oktas — the sky is completely covered by cloud with no blue sky visible. This is the maximum cloud amount. An overcast layer always constitutes a ceiling. VFR flight below an overcast layer requires sufficient clearance from the cloud base.

questions.question: In a METAR, wind is reported in:-
questions.explanation: In METARs and TAFs, wind direction is given in degrees true (not magnetic) and speed in knots. However, when ATC or ATIS gives the wind to a pilot, it is given in degrees magnetic (so the pilot can relate it directly to the runway heading). This is an important distinction.

questions.question: In a METAR, the cloud base height is reported as:-

options.text: height above aerodrome level in hundreds of feet

questions.explanation: Cloud base in a METAR is reported as height above aerodrome level (AAL) in hundreds of feet. For example, SCT015 means scattered cloud at 1500 ft above the aerodrome. To get the cloud base AMSL, add the aerodrome elevation. In TAFs, cloud is also reported as height AAL.

questions.question: A katabatic wind is:-

options.text: a cold wind that flows downslope at night
a warm wind that flows upslope during the day

questions.explanation: A katabatic wind flows downslope at night when the mountain surface cools by radiation, cooling the air in contact with it. This cold, dense air sinks downhill under gravity. Katabatic winds can be strong in valleys and can cause frost pockets in low-lying areas where the cold air pools.

questions.question: Clear ice forms on an aircraft when:-

options.text: large supercooled water droplets strike the aircraft and spread before freezing
small droplets freeze instantly on contact
the aircraft flies through cirrus cloud

questions.explanation: Clear (glaze) ice forms from large supercooled water droplets (found in cumuliform clouds or freezing rain). The droplets are large enough to flow over the surface before freezing, forming a smooth, clear, hard layer of ice. Clear ice is the most dangerous type — it is heavy, hard to see, difficult to remove, and significantly alters the wing profile.

questions.question: The freezing level is the altitude at which the temperature is:-
questions.explanation: The freezing level is the altitude at which the free air temperature is 0°C. Above this level, supercooled water droplets can exist and airframe icing is possible. The freezing level varies with weather conditions and can be found from METARs (temperature), upper air charts, or calculated from surface temperature and lapse rate.

questions.question: Precipitation in the form of light drizzle can be expected from:-
questions.explanation: Drizzle consists of very small water droplets (less than 0.5 mm diameter) that fall slowly from low stratus or stratocumulus clouds. These clouds form in stable conditions with gentle uplift. Drizzle reduces visibility and can make runways slippery. Heavier precipitation requires deeper clouds with stronger updrafts.

questions.question: Frontal fog is found:-

options.text: at the centre of a high pressure system

questions.explanation: Frontal fog forms ahead of a warm front when warm rain falls through the cold air below. The rain evaporates into the cold air, saturating it and forming fog. This pre-frontal fog can extend 100-200 km ahead of the surface front and is particularly hazardous because it is combined with low cloud and poor visibility.

questions.question: Following the passage of a warm front in South Africa, the winds will:-
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, after a warm front passes, the wind backs (changes anticlockwise). For example, the wind may change from a northerly direction to a more north-westerly direction. The temperature increases, pressure stops falling (or falls more slowly), and visibility may be poor in the warm sector.

questions.question: A continental air mass:-

options.text: forms over the land and remains fairly dry throughout
forms over the ocean and is very moist

questions.explanation: A continental air mass forms over a large land area and has low moisture content because land surfaces provide little evaporation compared to oceans. In South Africa, tropical continental air from the interior is hot and dry. Maritime air masses, by contrast, form over oceans and are moist.

questions.question: Latent heat is:-

options.text: the heat released or absorbed during a change of state of water
the heat stored in the earth's surface
the heat lost by radiation at night

questions.explanation: Latent heat is the energy released or absorbed when water changes state — evaporation absorbs latent heat (cooling), condensation releases latent heat (warming). This is why the SALR is less than the DALR: condensation in rising saturated air releases latent heat, partially offsetting the cooling. Latent heat is a major energy source for thunderstorms.

questions.question: Orographic lift occurs when:-

options.text: air is forced to rise over a mountain or hill
air is heated by the sun and rises
air subsides in a high pressure system

questions.explanation: Orographic lift occurs when moving air encounters a mountain or hill and is forced to rise over it. As the air rises, it cools adiabatically. If it reaches its dewpoint, cloud forms on the windward side. The type of cloud depends on stability — stratiform in stable air, cumuliform in unstable air.

questions.question: Convective turbulence is most likely to occur:-

options.text: on hot afternoons over land with strong surface heating

questions.explanation: Convective (thermal) turbulence is caused by uneven surface heating. On hot afternoons, the sun heats the ground unevenly — dark surfaces, ploughed fields, and urban areas heat more than forests or water. Rising thermals and sinking air between them create bumpy conditions. It is worst in the early to mid-afternoon.

questions.question: Mechanical turbulence is caused by:-

options.text: wind flowing over rough terrain, buildings, or obstacles

questions.explanation: Mechanical turbulence results from friction between the wind and the earth's surface. Rough terrain, buildings, trees, and other obstacles disrupt the smooth flow of air, creating eddies and turbulence. It is strongest in strong winds over rough surfaces and decreases with altitude above the friction layer.

questions.question: A SIGMET is:-

options.text: a warning of significant meteorological hazards to all aircraft

questions.explanation: A SIGMET (Significant Meteorological Information) is an advisory warning of weather phenomena that may affect the safety of all aircraft. It covers: severe turbulence, severe icing, thunderstorms, volcanic ash, tropical cyclones, and other hazards. SIGMETs are issued for en-route weather, not for aerodrome weather.

questions.question: The trade winds in the Southern Hemisphere blow from the:-
questions.explanation: The trade winds blow from the subtropical high pressure belt toward the equatorial low (ITCZ). In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects them to the left, making them south-easterly. In the Northern Hemisphere, they are deflected to the right, making them north-easterly. Trade winds are generally steady and reliable.

questions.question: The pressure gradient force acts:-

options.text: from high pressure toward low pressure, perpendicular to the isobars
from low pressure toward high pressure

questions.explanation: The pressure gradient force (PGF) is the primary force that causes wind. It acts from high pressure toward low pressure, perpendicular to the isobars. The closer the isobars are together (steeper gradient), the stronger the PGF and the stronger the wind. The Coriolis force then deflects this flow.

questions.question: Closely spaced isobars on a weather chart indicate:-
questions.explanation: Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient — a large pressure change over a short distance. This produces a strong pressure gradient force and therefore strong winds. Widely spaced isobars indicate a gentle gradient and light winds. This is one of the most important features to identify on a synoptic chart.

questions.question: An isobar is a line on a weather chart joining places of:-
questions.explanation: An isobar is a line connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure (reduced to mean sea level). Isobars are drawn at intervals of 4 hPa on synoptic charts. Their spacing indicates wind strength and their pattern reveals pressure systems (highs, lows, troughs, ridges, cols).

questions.question: An isotherm is a line on a weather chart joining places of:-
questions.explanation: An isotherm connects points of equal temperature. Isotherms are used on upper air charts and surface analysis charts to show temperature distribution. Closely packed isotherms indicate a strong temperature gradient, which is often associated with frontal zones.

questions.question: When flying from warm air to cold air without updating the altimeter setting:-

options.text: the altimeter will over-read (indicate higher than actual altitude)

questions.explanation: Cold air is denser and the pressure levels are lower (compressed). Flying from warm to cold air, the aircraft descends with the pressure levels but the altimeter still reads the warm-air altitude — it over-reads. 'High to Low (temperature), look out below.' The aircraft is lower than indicated.

questions.question: The transition altitude in South Africa is:-

options.text: the altitude above which flight levels are used (varies by airspace)
the altitude where temperature stops decreasing

questions.explanation: The transition altitude is the altitude at or below which aircraft use QNH (altitude AMSL) and above which they use the standard pressure setting 1013.25 hPa (flight levels). In South Africa, the transition altitude varies depending on the airspace and is published in the AIP. Above it, all aircraft use the same pressure reference for vertical separation.

questions.question: The dewpoint temperature of an air parcel:-

options.text: decreases slowly as the air rises (approximately 0.5°C per 1000 ft)
decreases at the same rate as the DALR

questions.explanation: As unsaturated air rises, the dewpoint decreases at approximately 0.5°C per 1000 ft (the dewpoint lapse rate). The air temperature decreases at 3°C per 1000 ft (DALR). Since temperature drops faster than dewpoint, they converge — the difference closes at about 2.5°C per 1000 ft. When they meet, condensation occurs (cloud base).

questions.question: Carburettor icing is indicated by:-

options.text: a rough running engine and a gradual decrease in RPM

questions.explanation: Carburettor ice restricts the air intake, reducing the fuel/air mixture entering the engine. This causes a gradual drop in RPM (fixed pitch) or manifold pressure (CSU), and the engine runs rough. If not treated with carburettor heat, the ice can completely block the intake and cause engine failure.

questions.question: The weather condition associated with a surface temperature inversion is:-

options.text: an increase in temperature with altitude

questions.explanation: A surface temperature inversion occurs when the temperature increases with altitude near the surface (opposite of normal). It is very stable, trapping moisture, smoke, and pollutants below it. This produces fog, mist, haze, poor visibility, and smooth flying conditions. Inversions commonly form on clear, calm nights by radiative cooling.

questions.question: Subsidence in the atmosphere is associated with:-

options.text: high pressure systems, warming, and suppressed cloud formation
low pressure systems and heavy rain

questions.explanation: Subsidence is the large-scale sinking of air, typically in high pressure systems (anticyclones). As air descends, it compresses and warms adiabatically. This warming dries the air and suppresses cloud formation, producing fine weather. A subsidence inversion can form, trapping pollution and moisture below it.

questions.question: The Hadley Cell is a global circulation pattern in which:-

options.text: warm air rises at the equator and sinks at about 30° latitude
cold air rises at the poles and sinks at the equator
air flows directly from the poles to the equator
air circulates only in the stratosphere

questions.explanation: The Hadley Cell is a tropical circulation: intense solar heating at the equator causes air to rise (forming the ITCZ), flow poleward at altitude, cool and sink at about 30° latitude (forming the subtropical high pressure belt), and return to the equator as the trade winds. This is the primary driver of tropical weather.

questions.question: The subtropical high pressure belt is located at approximately:-
questions.explanation: The subtropical high pressure belt (horse latitudes) lies at approximately 30°N and 30°S. It is caused by the descending limb of the Hadley Cell. Air subsides, warms, and produces generally fine, dry weather. The world's major deserts (Sahara, Kalahari, Australian) lie under this belt. South Africa is influenced by the South Atlantic and South Indian Ocean highs.

questions.question: The effect of altitude on air pressure is that pressure:-
questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above to exert weight. The rate of decrease is not linear — it decreases more rapidly at lower altitudes (approximately 1 hPa per 30 ft near sea level). At 18,000 ft, pressure is approximately half the sea level value.

questions.question: A col on a synoptic chart is:-

options.text: a neutral area between two highs and two lows
a strong ridge of high pressure

questions.explanation: A col is a region of almost flat pressure gradient between two highs and two lows arranged alternately. Winds are light and variable in a col. Weather in a col is unpredictable — it can be fine or can develop fog (in winter) or thunderstorms (in summer) due to the lack of wind to disperse moisture or heat.

questions.question: Turbulence encountered in clear air at high altitude, often near jet streams, is called:-
questions.explanation: Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) occurs at high altitude in cloud-free conditions, typically near jet streams, troughs, and areas of strong wind shear. It cannot be detected visually or by weather radar, making it particularly hazardous. It is caused by wind shear between air masses moving at different speeds.

questions.question: The TEMPO group in a TAF indicates:-

options.text: temporary fluctuations in weather conditions expected to last less than one hour at a time
conditions expected for the entire forecast period

questions.explanation: TEMPO indicates temporary fluctuations from the prevailing conditions that are expected to occur for periods of less than one hour at a time and in total cover less than half the forecast period. For example, TEMPO 1215/1218 RA means temporary rain expected between 1500Z and 1800Z.

questions.question: The BECMG group in a TAF indicates:-

options.text: a gradual or permanent change to new prevailing conditions

questions.explanation: BECMG (becoming) indicates a gradual change to new prevailing conditions expected to occur during the specified time period. Once the change is complete, the new conditions become the prevailing forecast. For example, BECMG 1012/1014 means conditions will change between 1200Z and 1400Z.

questions.question: Visibility in a METAR is reported in:-
questions.explanation: In ICAO METARs (used in South Africa), visibility is reported in metres. A visibility of 9999 means 10 km or more. Values below 5000 m are reported in steps of 100 m; between 5000 and 9000 m in steps of 1000 m. If CAVOK applies, the visibility group is replaced by CAVOK.

questions.question: The PROB group in a TAF indicates:-

options.text: the probability (usually 30% or 40%) of a weather event occurring

questions.explanation: PROB30 or PROB40 in a TAF indicates a 30% or 40% probability of the specified weather occurring during the given time period. PROB30 means unlikely but possible; PROB40 means a reasonable chance. Probabilities below 30% or above 50% are not used — above 50% would be included in the main forecast.

questions.question: The three main methods of heat transfer in the atmosphere are:-
questions.explanation: Heat is transferred in the atmosphere by: (1) Radiation — electromagnetic waves (how the sun heats the earth), (2) Conduction — direct contact (how the ground heats the air touching it), (3) Convection — vertical movement of heated air (thermals). Advection is horizontal heat transfer by wind movement.

questions.question: The atmosphere is primarily heated by:-

options.text: terrestrial radiation from the earth's surface

questions.explanation: The atmosphere is largely transparent to short-wave solar radiation, which passes through and heats the earth's surface. The warmed surface then re-radiates energy as long-wave (terrestrial/infrared) radiation, which is absorbed by water vapour and CO₂ in the atmosphere. This is why temperature decreases with altitude — the heat source is at the bottom.

questions.question: The diurnal variation of temperature is greatest:-

options.text: over land on clear days with light winds
on overcast days with strong winds

questions.explanation: Diurnal (daily) temperature range is greatest over land on clear days with light winds. Clear skies allow maximum solar heating by day and maximum radiative cooling at night. Light winds mean less mixing to moderate extremes. Land heats and cools faster than water. Overcast skies and strong winds reduce the diurnal range.

questions.question: The maximum surface temperature on a clear day typically occurs at approximately:-
questions.explanation: Although the sun is highest at noon, the surface continues to absorb more heat than it radiates until about 1400-1500 local time. After this, outgoing radiation exceeds incoming, and the surface begins to cool. The minimum temperature occurs just after sunrise, when the surface has been cooling all night.

questions.question: The minimum surface temperature on a clear night typically occurs at approximately:-
questions.explanation: The surface continues to lose heat by radiation throughout the night. The minimum temperature occurs just after sunrise because, although the sun has risen, the initial weak solar radiation is not yet enough to offset the ongoing radiative cooling. Shortly after sunrise, incoming radiation exceeds outgoing and the surface begins to warm.

questions.question: Specific humidity is:-

options.text: the mass of water vapour per unit mass of air
the ratio of actual vapour to maximum possible
the temperature at which air becomes saturated
the amount of rainfall per hour

questions.explanation: Specific humidity is the mass of water vapour contained in a unit mass of air (grams per kilogram). Unlike relative humidity, specific humidity does not change with temperature — it only changes when moisture is added or removed. It is a useful measure for tracking moisture content of an air mass.

questions.question: For cloud to form, the air must be:-

options.text: cooled to its dewpoint and condensation nuclei must be present

questions.explanation: Cloud formation requires three conditions: (1) The air must be cooled to its dewpoint (saturation), (2) Condensation nuclei must be present (tiny particles like dust, salt, or smoke for water to condense onto), (3) There must be a lifting mechanism (convection, orographic, frontal, or convergence). Without nuclei, supersaturation can occur.

questions.question: The four main lifting mechanisms that cause cloud formation are:-
questions.explanation: Air can be lifted to form clouds by: (1) Convection — surface heating creates thermals, (2) Orographic — air forced over mountains, (3) Frontal — warm air rises over cold air at fronts, (4) Convergence — air masses flowing together force air upward. Each mechanism produces different cloud types depending on stability.

questions.question: Stratocumulus cloud is:-

options.text: a low-level cloud appearing as a grey or white layer with rounded masses or rolls
a cloud of great vertical development

questions.explanation: Stratocumulus is a low-level cloud (below 6500 ft) that appears as a layer of rounded masses, rolls, or patches. It is grey or white with darker parts. It forms in stable to slightly unstable conditions and may produce light drizzle. It is one of the most common cloud types worldwide.

questions.question: Cirrostratus cloud is characterised by:-

options.text: a thin, whitish veil that often produces a halo around the sun or moon

questions.explanation: Cirrostratus is a high-level (above 20,000 ft) thin, whitish cloud sheet composed of ice crystals. It often covers the entire sky and produces a characteristic halo (ring) around the sun or moon. Cirrostratus thickening is a classic sign of an approaching warm front.

questions.question: Hail is most commonly associated with:-
questions.explanation: Hail forms in cumulonimbus clouds with very strong updrafts. Ice particles are carried up and down within the cloud, accumulating layers of ice each time they pass through the supercooled water zone. When they become too heavy for the updraft to support, they fall as hail. Larger hail requires stronger updrafts.

questions.question: Freezing rain occurs when:-

options.text: rain falls through a layer of sub-zero air and freezes on contact with the aircraft or ground

questions.explanation: Freezing rain forms when rain (liquid water) falls from a warm layer aloft through a shallow layer of sub-zero air near the surface. The drops remain liquid (supercooled) and freeze on contact with any surface at or below 0°C. It produces clear ice — the most dangerous form of icing, capable of rapid ice accumulation.

questions.question: The effect of icing on an aircraft includes:-

options.text: increased weight, increased drag, decreased lift, and possible engine failure

questions.explanation: Airframe icing has multiple dangerous effects: increased weight (reduces performance), increased drag (disrupted airflow over wings), decreased lift (altered wing profile), increased stall speed, blocked pitot tubes and static ports (erroneous instrument readings), restricted engine air intake, and impaired visibility through the windscreen.

questions.question: During the South African winter, weather is primarily influenced by:-

options.text: cold fronts moving from west to east across the southern part of the country

questions.explanation: During winter (May-September), the westerly wind belt and its associated cold fronts shift northward, affecting the southern and western parts of South Africa. The Cape receives most of its rainfall from these fronts. The interior is generally dry and cold with frost on the highveld. Berg winds precede the fronts.

questions.question: The South African highveld experiences afternoon thunderstorms in summer primarily due to:-

options.text: strong surface heating combined with moisture from the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: In summer, the highveld (interior plateau at ~5000 ft) heats strongly during the day. Moist south-easterly trade winds bring moisture from the Indian Ocean. The combination of surface heating (convection trigger) and available moisture produces afternoon cumulonimbus development and thunderstorms, often with hail on the highveld.

questions.question: The Western Cape receives most of its rainfall in:-
questions.explanation: The Western Cape has a Mediterranean climate — winter rainfall region. Cold fronts from the westerly wind belt bring rain during winter (May-August). In summer, the South Atlantic High moves south, blocking fronts from reaching the Cape. This makes the Western Cape dry in summer and wet in winter — opposite to the rest of South Africa.

questions.question: Upslope fog forms when:-

options.text: moist air is forced up a slope and cools to its dewpoint
the ground cools by radiation at night
warm air moves over a cold surface

questions.explanation: Upslope fog forms when moist air is carried up a gradual slope by the wind. As it rises, it cools adiabatically. If it cools to its dewpoint, fog forms. This type of fog can be persistent and widespread, covering large areas of elevated terrain. It requires a gentle slope and steady wind.

questions.question: Radiation fog is most likely to dissipate:-

options.text: after sunrise when solar heating warms the ground and air
when the wind increases to gale force

questions.explanation: Radiation fog dissipates when the sun heats the ground, which warms the air in contact with it above the dewpoint. The fog 'burns off' from the ground up, often lifting to form a layer of low stratus before clearing completely. Thin fog clears quickly; thick fog may persist until late morning. Increasing wind can also disperse it.

questions.question: Steam fog (arctic sea smoke) forms when:-

options.text: very cold air moves over a relatively warm water surface
warm air moves over a cold surface

questions.explanation: Steam fog forms when very cold air passes over a much warmer water surface. The water evaporates rapidly into the cold air, immediately saturating it and forming fog that rises in wisps like steam. It is common over lakes and rivers in autumn/winter when the water is still warm but the air has become very cold.

questions.question: The Bergeron process of precipitation formation involves:-

options.text: ice crystals growing at the expense of supercooled water droplets in mixed clouds
large droplets colliding with smaller ones

questions.explanation: The Bergeron (ice crystal) process occurs in clouds containing both ice crystals and supercooled water droplets (mixed clouds). Because the saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over water, water vapour migrates from the droplets to the ice crystals, which grow rapidly. When heavy enough, they fall as snow (melting to rain if they pass through warm air).

questions.question: The collision-coalescence process of precipitation formation occurs in:-

options.text: warm clouds (entirely above 0°C) where large droplets collide with and absorb smaller ones

questions.explanation: In warm clouds (tops above 0°C), precipitation forms by the collision-coalescence process. Larger droplets fall faster than smaller ones, colliding with and absorbing them, growing progressively larger. This process is common in tropical regions where cloud tops may not reach the freezing level. It produces warm rain.

questions.question: Sleet is:-

options.text: partially melted snow or a mixture of rain and snow

questions.explanation: Sleet consists of ice pellets formed when snowflakes fall through a warm layer (melting partially or completely) and then refreeze in a cold layer near the surface. It can also refer to a mixture of rain and snow. Sleet indicates a warm layer aloft and a cold layer near the surface — conditions that may also produce freezing rain.

questions.question: The wind direction given by ATC on the radio is in:-
questions.explanation: When ATC or ATIS gives wind information verbally to a pilot, the direction is in degrees magnetic. This allows the pilot to directly compare it with the runway heading (also magnetic). Written reports (METARs, TAFs) use degrees true. This is an important distinction that pilots must remember.

questions.question: A SPECI report is:-

options.text: a special METAR issued when weather conditions change significantly

questions.explanation: A SPECI (special) is an unscheduled METAR issued when significant changes occur between routine observations. Triggers include: wind shift, visibility dropping below or improving through specified values, cloud base changes, onset or cessation of significant weather (thunderstorms, freezing precipitation), or any other operationally significant change.

questions.question: The altimeter setting that will cause the altimeter to read aerodrome elevation on the ground is:-
questions.explanation: QNH is the pressure setting that, when set on the altimeter subscale, causes the altimeter to read the aerodrome elevation when the aircraft is on the ground. It is the atmospheric pressure at mean sea level for that location. QFE would read zero on the ground; 1013.25 hPa would read pressure altitude.

questions.question: A gust is defined as:-

options.text: a rapid, short-term increase in wind speed above the mean

questions.explanation: A gust is a sudden, brief increase in wind speed. In METARs, gusts are reported when the peak speed exceeds the mean by 10 kt or more (e.g., 25015G30KT means wind 250° at 15 kt gusting to 30 kt). Gusts are caused by turbulent mixing and are most common in unstable conditions with strong winds.

questions.question: A squall line is:-

options.text: a line of thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front
a line of clear air turbulence

questions.explanation: A squall line is a narrow band of active thunderstorms that often forms ahead of (or along) a cold front. It can extend for hundreds of kilometres and produce severe weather — heavy rain, hail, strong gusty winds, turbulence, and wind shear. Squall lines are particularly hazardous because they present a continuous barrier of bad weather.

questions.question: The anvil shape at the top of a mature cumulonimbus cloud is caused by:-

options.text: the cloud top spreading out when it reaches the tropopause or a stable layer

questions.explanation: The anvil (incus) forms when the rising air in a Cb reaches the tropopause or a strong stable layer and can no longer rise. It spreads out horizontally, often in the direction of the upper winds, forming the characteristic anvil shape. The anvil is composed of ice crystals and indicates a mature or dissipating thunderstorm.

questions.question: Lightning is caused by:-

options.text: the discharge of electrical potential built up between different parts of a cloud or between the cloud and ground

questions.explanation: Lightning is a massive electrical discharge. Within a Cb, charge separation occurs — positive charges accumulate near the top and negative charges near the base. When the potential difference becomes great enough, a discharge occurs (cloud-to-cloud, cloud-to-ground, or within the cloud). Lightning can damage aircraft and temporarily blind pilots.

questions.question: Dew forms when:-

options.text: the surface temperature cools to the dewpoint and the dewpoint is above 0°C

questions.explanation: Dew forms on surfaces that cool by radiation to the dewpoint temperature, provided the dewpoint is above 0°C. Water vapour condenses directly onto the cold surface as liquid droplets. If the dewpoint is below 0°C, the water vapour deposits as frost (ice crystals) instead of dew. Dew typically forms on clear, calm nights.

questions.question: Frost forms on surfaces when:-

options.text: the surface temperature cools below 0°C and below the dewpoint
the wind speed is above 20 knots

questions.explanation: Frost forms by sublimation — water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals on surfaces that have cooled below 0°C and below the dewpoint (frost point). This occurs on clear, calm nights with high humidity. Frost on aircraft wings must be completely removed before flight as it disrupts airflow and significantly increases the stall speed.

questions.question: At FL100, the ISA temperature is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at any altitude = 15°C - (2°C × altitude in thousands of feet). At FL100 (10,000 ft): 15 - (2 × 10) = 15 - 20 = -5°C. This calculation is essential for determining ISA deviation, density altitude, and true airspeed corrections.

questions.question: At FL050, the ISA temperature is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at FL050 (5,000 ft): 15°C - (2°C × 5) = 15 - 10 = +5°C. The ISA lapse rate of 2°C per 1000 ft is used from sea level up to the tropopause (36,090 ft). Above the tropopause, ISA temperature remains constant at -56.5°C.

questions.question: If the OAT at FL080 is +10°C, the ISA deviation is:-
questions.explanation: ISA temperature at FL080 (8,000 ft) = 15 - (2 × 8) = 15 - 16 = -1°C. Actual OAT = +10°C. ISA deviation = actual - ISA = +10 - (-1) = +11°C. The air is 11°C warmer than standard, meaning higher density altitude and reduced aircraft performance.

questions.question: The 1 in 60 rule for pressure changes states that near sea level, a change of 1 hPa corresponds to approximately:-
questions.explanation: Near sea level, a pressure change of 1 hPa corresponds to approximately 30 ft (27 ft to be precise) of altitude change. This is useful for estimating altimeter errors. For example, if the QNH is 3 hPa lower than set, the aircraft is approximately 90 ft lower than indicated.

questions.question: When an aircraft is parked overnight and the altimeter reads lower than the aerodrome elevation the next morning (with QNH unchanged), this indicates:-

options.text: the atmospheric pressure has increased overnight

questions.explanation: If the altimeter reads lower than the aerodrome elevation with the same QNH set, the actual pressure has risen. Higher pressure pushes the pressure levels up, but the altimeter still uses the old (lower) QNH — so it under-reads. Updating the QNH to the current (higher) value would correct the reading back to aerodrome elevation.

questions.question: The Beaufort Scale is used to estimate:-

options.text: wind speed based on observed effects on the sea or land

questions.explanation: The Beaufort Scale relates wind speed to observed conditions. It ranges from Force 0 (calm, <1 kt) to Force 12 (hurricane, >64 kt). At sea, it uses wave height and appearance. On land, it uses effects like smoke drift, tree movement, and structural damage. It is useful when no anemometer is available.

questions.question: Turbulence associated with a temperature inversion is most likely at:-

options.text: the top of the inversion layer where wind shear may occur

questions.explanation: At the top of a temperature inversion, there is often a significant change in wind speed and/or direction (wind shear). This shear can produce moderate to severe turbulence at the inversion boundary. Below the inversion, conditions are typically smooth (stable). Above it, conditions depend on the upper atmosphere stability.

questions.question: The rotor zone in mountain wave conditions is located:-

options.text: below the wave crests on the lee side of the mountain
on the windward side of the mountain

questions.explanation: The rotor zone is the most turbulent part of a mountain wave system. It is located below the wave crests on the lee (downwind) side of the mountain, typically between the surface and the mountain top height. Rotor turbulence can be severe to extreme and is indicated by ragged rotor clouds (if moisture is present).

questions.question: The Benguela Current along the west coast of South Africa is:-

options.text: a cold ocean current that promotes fog and low cloud along the coast
a warm current that brings tropical storms
a seasonal current that only flows in summer

questions.explanation: The Benguela Current is a cold ocean current flowing northward along the west coast of South Africa. When warm, moist air from the Atlantic passes over this cold water, it is cooled to its dewpoint, forming advection fog and low stratus cloud. This makes the west coast prone to fog, particularly in summer.

questions.question: The Agulhas Current along the east coast of South Africa is:-

options.text: a warm ocean current that provides moisture for weather systems
a cold current that causes fog
a weak current with no weather significance
a current that flows only in winter

questions.explanation: The Agulhas Current is a warm, fast-flowing current along the east coast of South Africa. It provides moisture and warmth to air masses passing over it, contributing to the moist conditions along the KZN coast. The warm water also enhances instability in polar maritime air masses moving northward, intensifying weather systems.

questions.question: A pilot report (PIREP) provides:-

options.text: actual weather conditions encountered by an aircraft in flight

questions.explanation: A PIREP (Pilot Report) is a report of actual weather conditions encountered by a pilot during flight. It includes: position, time, altitude, aircraft type, and observed conditions (turbulence, icing, cloud tops/bases, visibility, wind). PIREPs are valuable because they provide real-time data from the actual flight environment.

questions.question: The Coriolis force is zero at:-
questions.explanation: The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and increases with latitude, reaching maximum at the poles. This is because the Coriolis force depends on the component of the earth's rotation perpendicular to the surface, which is zero at the equator. Near the equator, wind flows more directly from high to low pressure.

questions.question: Divergence is associated with:-

options.text: subsiding air, high pressure, and generally stable conditions

questions.explanation: Divergence occurs when air flows outward from a region. At the surface, this outflow must be replaced by air subsiding from above. Subsiding air warms adiabatically and suppresses cloud formation. Divergence is associated with high pressure systems (anticyclones), fine weather, and stable conditions.

questions.question: The prevailing westerly winds are found at approximately:-
questions.explanation: The prevailing westerlies blow from the subtropical high pressure belt (~30°) toward the sub-polar low (~60°). In the Southern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects them to the left, making them north-westerly to westerly. These westerlies drive the cold fronts and weather systems that affect southern South Africa, particularly in winter.

questions.question: The polar front is located at approximately:-

options.text: 60° latitude, where polar and tropical air masses meet
