questions.explanation: The polar front is the boundary between cold polar air and warmer tropical air at approximately 60° latitude. It is a zone of convergence where mid-latitude depressions (cyclones) form and develop. The polar front is not fixed — it migrates north and south with the seasons, bringing frontal weather to different latitudes.

questions.question: When pressure falls, the altimeter (with QNH unchanged) will:-
questions.explanation: If pressure falls and the QNH is not updated, the altimeter over-reads — it shows a higher altitude than the aircraft's actual altitude. The aircraft has descended with the falling pressure levels but the altimeter doesn't know this. This is the 'high to low, look out below' principle applied to pressure changes over time.

questions.question: The weather phenomenon known as 'line storms' in South Africa refers to:-

options.text: a line of thunderstorms that develops along a convergence zone or trough
a line of fog along the coast
a line of high pressure systems
a line of clear air turbulence

questions.explanation: Line storms in South Africa are lines of thunderstorms that develop along convergence zones, troughs, or pre-frontal troughs. They are common over the highveld in summer and can produce severe weather including heavy rain, hail, strong winds, and tornadoes. They present a continuous barrier of dangerous weather to aviation.

questions.question: The effect of flying from low to high pressure without updating the altimeter is:-

options.text: the altimeter under-reads (aircraft is higher than indicated)

questions.explanation: Flying from low to high pressure without updating QNH causes the altimeter to under-read — the aircraft is actually higher than indicated. This is the reverse of 'high to low, look out below.' While less dangerous for terrain clearance, it means the aircraft is not at the assigned altitude, affecting vertical separation from other traffic.

questions.question: Supercooled water droplets are:-

options.text: liquid water droplets that exist at temperatures below 0°C

questions.explanation: Supercooled water droplets are liquid water that remains unfrozen at temperatures below 0°C. They can exist down to about -40°C. They freeze instantly on contact with any surface (such as an aircraft), making them the primary cause of airframe icing. They are found in clouds at temperatures between 0°C and -40°C.

questions.question: Mixed icing occurs when:-

options.text: both rime and clear ice form simultaneously on the aircraft
ice forms only on the propeller
ice forms inside the carburettor only

questions.explanation: Mixed icing is a combination of rime and clear ice forming at the same time. It occurs when the cloud contains a mixture of small and large supercooled water droplets. The result is a rough, irregular ice formation that is difficult to remove and significantly degrades aerodynamic performance. It is common at temperatures between -10°C and -15°C.

questions.question: The most severe airframe icing is typically found at temperatures between:-
questions.explanation: The most severe icing occurs between 0°C and -20°C because this is where the highest concentration of supercooled water droplets exists. Below -20°C, most water has already frozen into ice crystals (which generally bounce off the aircraft). The worst icing zone is often around -5°C to -15°C in cumuliform clouds.

questions.question: Light turbulence is defined as turbulence that:-

options.text: causes slight, erratic changes in altitude and/or attitude
causes large, abrupt changes in altitude

questions.explanation: Turbulence intensity categories: Light — slight, erratic changes in altitude/attitude, occupants may feel slight strain against seat belts. Moderate — changes in altitude/attitude, occupants feel definite strain. Severe — large, abrupt changes, aircraft may be momentarily out of control. Extreme — aircraft is violently tossed, practically impossible to control.

questions.question: The term 'ceiling' in aviation meteorology refers to:-

options.text: the height of the lowest layer of cloud covering more than half the sky (BKN or OVC)
the maximum altitude an aircraft can reach

questions.explanation: A ceiling is the height above ground of the lowest layer of cloud reported as broken (BKN, 5-7 oktas) or overcast (OVC, 8 oktas). Scattered (SCT) and few (FEW) layers do not constitute a ceiling. The ceiling is critical for VFR operations as it determines whether visual flight is possible.

questions.question: The minimum visibility for VFR flight in uncontrolled airspace (Class G) below 10,000 ft in South Africa is:-
questions.explanation: In South African Class G (uncontrolled) airspace below FL100, the minimum flight visibility for VFR is 5 km. The pilot must also remain clear of cloud with the surface in sight. These minima ensure adequate see-and-avoid capability. In controlled airspace, the requirements may be different.

questions.question: A warm sector is the area:-

options.text: between a warm front and the following cold front in a depression
at the centre of a high pressure system
ahead of a warm front only

questions.explanation: The warm sector is the area of warm air between the warm front (ahead) and the cold front (behind) in a mid-latitude depression. Weather in the warm sector typically includes: low stratus or stratocumulus, poor visibility (haze, mist, drizzle), warm temperatures, and relatively steady conditions until the cold front arrives.

questions.question: The life cycle of a mid-latitude depression includes the stages:-
questions.explanation: A mid-latitude depression develops through: (1) Wave stage — a small wave forms on the polar front, (2) Young stage — warm and cold fronts develop, pressure falls, (3) Mature stage — deepest pressure, strongest winds, well-defined fronts, (4) Occluding stage — cold front catches warm front, warm air lifted off surface, system weakens.

questions.question: The weather associated with the passage of a cold front typically includes:-

options.text: a sudden wind shift, drop in temperature, rise in pressure, and clearing skies

questions.explanation: Cold front passage brings: sudden wind shift (backing in SH), temperature drop, pressure rise, heavy showers or thunderstorms (brief but intense), turbulence, and then clearing skies as the cold air moves in. The weather band is narrow (50-100 km) but intense compared to the gradual, widespread weather of a warm front.

questions.question: Altocumulus castellanus clouds indicate:-

options.text: instability at medium levels and potential thunderstorm development
the approach of a warm front

questions.explanation: Altocumulus castellanus (ACC) are medium-level clouds with turret-like protrusions rising from a common base, resembling castle battlements. They indicate instability at medium levels (6500-20000 ft) and are often a precursor to afternoon thunderstorm development. If seen in the morning, thunderstorms are likely later in the day.

questions.question: Mammatus clouds are associated with:-

options.text: severe turbulence and are often seen on the underside of cumulonimbus anvils

questions.explanation: Mammatus clouds are pouch-like protrusions hanging from the underside of a cloud (usually a Cb anvil). They are formed by sinking air and indicate severe turbulence, strong downdrafts, and potentially severe weather nearby. While visually dramatic, they are a warning sign to avoid the area.

questions.question: The main weather hazards for general aviation include:-

options.text: low cloud, poor visibility, thunderstorms, icing, turbulence, and wind shear

questions.explanation: The main weather hazards for GA pilots are: low cloud and poor visibility (VFR into IMC is a leading cause of fatal accidents), thunderstorms (turbulence, hail, lightning, microbursts), icing (airframe and carburettor), turbulence (mechanical, convective, mountain wave), wind shear, and density altitude effects on performance.

questions.question: VFR flight into IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) is dangerous because:-

options.text: a VFR pilot may lose spatial orientation and control of the aircraft without visual references

questions.explanation: VFR into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatal GA accidents. Without visual references (horizon, ground), a non-instrument-rated pilot quickly loses spatial orientation. The vestibular system gives false sensations, leading to unusual attitudes, spiral dives, or stalls. Average survival time for a VFR pilot in IMC is estimated at 178 seconds.

questions.question: The wind reported in a METAR as VRB02KT means:-

options.text: wind veering at 2 knots per minute

questions.explanation: VRB indicates variable wind direction. This is used when the wind speed is 3 kt or less, or when the direction varies by 180° or more. VRB02KT means the wind direction is variable (no consistent direction) at 2 knots. This typically indicates very light, shifting winds.

questions.question: The abbreviation CB in a METAR or TAF refers to:-
questions.explanation: CB in weather reports indicates cumulonimbus cloud — the thunderstorm cloud. When CB is reported, it warns of potential severe weather: heavy rain, hail, lightning, severe turbulence, wind shear, and microbursts. CB is always reported in METARs and TAFs regardless of the cloud amount, due to its significance.

questions.question: The abbreviation TCU in a METAR refers to:-
questions.explanation: TCU stands for towering cumulus — a cumulus cloud with significant vertical development that has not yet reached the cumulonimbus stage. TCU indicates active convection and potential for thunderstorm development. Like CB, TCU is always reported in METARs and TAFs due to its significance for aviation.

questions.question: The temperature at which all water droplets in a cloud will have frozen into ice crystals is approximately:-
questions.explanation: At approximately -40°C, all supercooled water droplets spontaneously freeze (homogeneous nucleation). Above this temperature, supercooled droplets can coexist with ice crystals. Below -40°C, clouds consist entirely of ice crystals, and airframe icing from supercooled water is no longer a risk (though ice crystal icing can still occur in jet engines).

questions.question: The South Indian Ocean High pressure system affects South Africa by:-

options.text: driving moist south-easterly trade winds over the eastern parts of the country
bringing cold fronts to the Western Cape
producing fog along the west coast only

questions.explanation: The South Indian Ocean High is a semi-permanent anticyclone east of South Africa. Its anticlockwise circulation (Southern Hemisphere) drives moist south-easterly trade winds over the eastern parts of South Africa, providing the moisture for summer thunderstorms over the interior. Its position and strength influence the country's weather patterns significantly.

questions.question: The South Atlantic High pressure system affects South Africa by:-

options.text: influencing the weather of the Western Cape and driving the south-easterly winds around the Cape
bringing moisture to the interior only
producing coastal lows on the east coast

questions.explanation: The South Atlantic High is a semi-permanent anticyclone west of South Africa. It drives the south-easterly winds around the Cape (including the Black South Easter). In summer, it moves south and blocks cold fronts from reaching the Western Cape. In winter, it moves north, allowing fronts through. It also contributes to the Benguela Current's cold water upwelling.

questions.question: Tropical cyclones that may affect the east coast of South Africa typically form over:-

options.text: the warm waters of the south-west Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones affecting South Africa's east coast form over the warm waters (>26.5°C) of the south-west Indian Ocean, typically between Madagascar and the African mainland. They can bring destructive winds, heavy rainfall, flooding, and storm surge to the KZN and Mozambique coasts. They are most common from November to April.

questions.question: A thermal is:-

options.text: a rising column of warm air caused by uneven surface heating

questions.explanation: A thermal is a column of rising warm air created when the sun heats the ground unevenly. Dark surfaces (ploughed fields, tarmac, rocky ground) heat more than light surfaces (water, forests). The warm air rises, and if it reaches its dewpoint, a cumulus cloud forms at the top. Thermals cause convective turbulence for aircraft and are used by glider pilots for soaring.

questions.question: The effect of a headwind on take-off performance is:-

options.text: a shorter take-off run and steeper climb gradient

questions.explanation: A headwind provides airspeed 'for free' — the aircraft reaches flying speed at a lower groundspeed, requiring less runway. The climb gradient over the ground is also steeper because the groundspeed is lower. This is why aircraft take off into the wind whenever possible. A tailwind has the opposite (detrimental) effect.

questions.question: High density altitude reduces aircraft performance because:-

options.text: the air is less dense, reducing lift, engine power, and propeller efficiency

questions.explanation: High density altitude means the air is less dense than standard. Less dense air means: less lift (wings produce less lift per unit area), less engine power (less air for combustion), less propeller efficiency (less air to accelerate). This results in longer take-off runs, reduced climb rates, and higher true airspeeds for the same indicated airspeed.

questions.question: The three factors that increase density altitude are:-

options.text: high elevation, high temperature, and high humidity
low elevation, low temperature, and low humidity
high pressure, low temperature, and low humidity
high wind speed, low cloud, and rain

questions.explanation: Density altitude increases with: (1) High elevation (less air above = lower pressure), (2) High temperature (warm air is less dense), (3) High humidity (water vapour is lighter than dry air). The combination of all three — a hot, humid day at a high-altitude aerodrome — produces the worst performance conditions. This is critical in South Africa's highveld.

questions.question: The weather abbreviation TS in a METAR indicates:-
questions.explanation: TS in a METAR or TAF indicates a thunderstorm. It may be combined with precipitation types: TSRA (thunderstorm with rain), TSGR (thunderstorm with hail), TSSN (thunderstorm with snow). A thunderstorm report always warrants caution — it indicates CB activity with associated hazards.

questions.question: The weather abbreviation FG in a METAR indicates:-
questions.explanation: FG in a METAR indicates fog — visibility less than 1000 m due to water droplets suspended near the surface. Related abbreviations: BR = mist (visibility 1000-5000 m), HZ = haze (dry particles), BCFG = patches of fog, PRFG = partial fog, VCFG = fog in the vicinity. Fog significantly affects aerodrome operations and may require instrument approaches.

questions.question: With reference to Station 6 of the Synoptic Station Models - 1, on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The present weather is:-
questions.explanation: Reading the present weather symbol from Station 6 on the Synoptic Weather Station Models chart, the symbol indicates moderate intermittent drizzle. Drizzle symbols use dots and commas, with the pattern indicating intensity (light/moderate/heavy) and continuity (intermittent/continuous).

questions.question: With reference to Station 2 of the Synoptic Station Models - 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The barometric tendency during the past three hours was:-
questions.explanation: The barometric tendency symbol at Station 2 shows the pressure trend over the past 3 hours. The symbol indicates the pressure was falling then became steady. Barometric tendency is shown by a line symbol to the right of the station circle, with the number indicating the magnitude of change in hPa.

questions.question: With reference to Station 4 of the Synoptic Station Models - 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The medium cloud indicated is:-
questions.explanation: The medium cloud symbol at Station 4 indicates thick altostratus or nimbostratus. Medium-level cloud types are plotted above and to the left of the station circle. Thick altostratus/nimbostratus is associated with continuous precipitation and poor visibility.

questions.question: With reference to Station 5 of the Synoptic Station Models - 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The pressure change during the past three hours was:-

options.text: A fall in pressure of 3 hPa
A rise in pressure of 3 hPa
A fall in pressure of 30 hPa
A rise in pressure of 0.3 hPa

questions.explanation: The pressure change value at Station 5 shows a fall of 3 hPa over the past three hours. The pressure change is indicated by the number next to the barometric tendency symbol, expressed in tenths of hPa (so '30' means 3.0 hPa). The tendency symbol shows the direction of change.

questions.question: With reference to Station 14 of the Synoptic Station Models - 2 on page 6 of the Meteorology Manual:-

options.text: The visibility is 200 metres in haze
The visibility is 2000 metres in fog
The visibility is 200 metres in mist
The visibility is 20 km in haze

questions.explanation: Reading Station 14 on the Synoptic Weather Station Models - 2 chart, the visibility value and present weather symbol indicate 200 metres visibility in haze. Haze is indicated by a specific synoptic symbol and reduces visibility due to dry particles (dust, smoke, etc.) suspended in the atmosphere.

questions.question: With reference to the TAF for Port Elizabeth (FAPE) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, an aircraft that intends landing between 1300 and 1500 local time would expect:-

options.text: 3 to 4 oktas of cloud at 1500 ft
5 to 7 oktas of cloud at 3000 ft
1 to 2 oktas of cloud at 2500 ft

questions.explanation: Reading the TAF for FAPE (Port Elizabeth), the forecast for the period covering 1300-1500 local time indicates SCT015, meaning scattered (3-4 oktas) cloud at 1500 ft. TAF times are in UTC, so local time must be converted (South Africa is UTC+2).

questions.question: With reference to the TAF for Durban (FADN) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, an aircraft landing between 1800 and 2000 local time would expect the surface wind to be:-
questions.explanation: Reading the TAF for FADN (Durban), the forecast wind for the period covering 1800-2000 local time is 140 degrees at 12 knots (140/12). Wind in TAFs is always given in degrees true and knots.

questions.question: With reference to the TAF for George (FAGG) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, the expected weather includes:-

options.text: Light rain temporarily becoming heavy rain between 1200 and 2000 local time
Continuous moderate rain throughout the day

questions.explanation: Reading the TAF for FAGG (George), the forecast includes light rain (RA) with a TEMPO group indicating temporarily heavy rain between 1200 and 2000 local time. TEMPO means the conditions are expected to occur temporarily during the specified period.

questions.question: With reference to the METAR for Johannesburg (FAJS) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual:-

options.text: The variation in the observed wind direction is between 350° and 070°
The cloud base is at 2500 ft

questions.explanation: Reading the METAR for FAJS (Johannesburg), the wind group includes a variable wind direction indicator showing the wind direction varies between 350° and 070°. Variable wind direction is reported when the wind direction fluctuates by 60° or more during the observation period.

questions.question: With reference to the METAR for George (FAGG) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual:-
questions.explanation: Reading the METAR for FAGG (George), the temperature/dew point group shows the dew point temperature is 15°C. In a METAR, temperature and dew point are reported as a pair separated by a slash (e.g., 18/15 means temperature 18°C, dew point 15°C).

questions.question: With reference to the METAR for Upington (FAUP) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual:-

options.text: There is no cloud below 5000 ft

questions.explanation: Reading the METAR for FAUP (Upington), the cloud group or CAVOK indicator shows there is no cloud below 5000 ft. CAVOK (Ceiling And Visibility OK) is used when visibility is 10 km or more, no cloud below 5000 ft or below the highest minimum sector altitude, no CB or TCU, and no significant weather.

questions.question: With reference to the METAR for Germiston (FAGM) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual:-

options.text: The METAR was taken on the 20th at 0730 local time
The METAR was taken on the 20th at 0530 UTC
The METAR was taken on the 7th at 0530 local time
The METAR was taken on the 20th at 0930 local time

questions.explanation: Reading the METAR for FAGM (Germiston), the date/time group indicates the observation was taken on the 20th day of the month at 0530 UTC, which is 0730 local time in South Africa (UTC+2). METAR times are always reported in UTC (Zulu time).

questions.question: With reference to the Significant Weather Chart 3 on page 15 of the Meteorology Manual. An aircraft intending to fly from Port Elizabeth (PE) along the coast towards Cape Town (CT) would experience:-

options.text: Initially drizzle from stratocumulus cloud becoming rain towards Cape Town
Fog along the coast clearing towards Cape Town

questions.explanation: Reading the Significant Weather Chart 3, the route from Port Elizabeth to Cape Town shows initially drizzle from stratocumulus cloud in the PE area, with conditions deteriorating to rain as the aircraft approaches Cape Town. Significant weather charts depict frontal positions, cloud types, precipitation, and other hazards.

questions.question: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The wind direction on the Natal North Coast at 5000 ft is:-
questions.explanation: Reading the Upper Winds and Temperatures chart, the spot wind for the Natal North Coast at 5000 ft shows a wind direction of 115° True. Upper wind charts show wind direction in degrees true and speed in knots at various flight levels and locations.

questions.question: With reference to the METAR for George (FAGG) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual:-

options.text: The visibility is 1000 m with fog in the vicinity
The visibility is 10 km with haze
The visibility is 5000 m with mist
The visibility is 500 m with fog

questions.explanation: Reading the METAR for FAGG (George), the visibility and weather groups indicate 1000 m visibility with fog in the vicinity (VCFG). The prefix VC means 'in the vicinity' — within 8 km of the aerodrome but not at the aerodrome itself.

questions.question: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The temperature at 5000 ft at S30° E015° is:-
questions.explanation: Reading the Upper Winds and Temperatures chart at the intersection of S30° and E015° at 5000 ft, the temperature deviation from ISA is +7°C. Temperatures on upper wind charts are expressed as deviations from ISA (International Standard Atmosphere) at the given altitude.

questions.question: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The wind direction and velocity (W/V) at 4000 ft at S25° E015° is:-
questions.explanation: Reading the Upper Winds and Temperatures chart at the intersection of S25° and E015° at 4000 ft, the wind direction is 221° True at 11 knots. Upper wind charts display spot winds as direction (degrees true) and speed (knots) at specific geographic coordinates and altitudes.
